According to a joint status report made public earlier, Apple said it is still waiting for Jon Prosser to provide additional documents and wants to depose Michael Ramacciotti again; both defendants also pushed back on how Apple has handled the case. Details below.

According to the joint status report filed with Judge James Donato, Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti are increasingly at odds over who is to blame for delays in a trade secrets lawsuit Apple filed against the two men in July 2025.

A bit of background

In short, shortly after unveiling iOS 26, Apple filed a trade secret misappropriation suit against Prosser and Ramacciotti after Prosser posted a video revealing a number of system details, including what ultimately turned out to be the Liquid Glass visual overhaul.

Apple alleged Ramacciotti improperly took a developer's iPhone from an employee who was later fired, and showed Prosser unreleased iOS features running on the device via FaceTime.

Since then, the case itself has seen its share of drama, including a clerk's default being entered against Prosser for failing to respond to Apple's complaint in time (though Prosser pushed back on claims he was ignoring the case).

About eight months later, the court agreed to vacate that default and give him another chance to formally answer the allegations.

Court filings show Ramaciotti, on the other hand, has answered Apple's complaint and largely complied with its document production requests.

However, since Prosser hired counsel and formally joined the case, things have taken a turn for the worse, with the three sides increasingly pointing fingers over who is responsible for the alleged trade secret disclosure and subsequent delays.

The latest joint status report

Returning to the latest status report, Apple said it wants Ramacciotti to update his written discovery responses and sit for another deposition to address what it described as inconsistencies with "Mr. Prosser's testimony."

Ramacciotti, however, said he is willing to sit for one more deposition as long as Apple provides "a roadmap of where this is going with respect to their claims, including what more (if anything) Apple needs from him."

As for Prosser, Apple said it is "still awaiting production of certain additional documents it requested over three months ago, including revenue reports and analytics for his YouTube channel, as well as communications with third parties as identified during his deposition."

Prosser pushed back, arguing that "the trade secrets at issue no longer appear to be trade secrets and have entered the public domain." In other words, his argument appears to be that because Apple has publicly released the iOS update with Liquid Glass, the information central to the case is now publicly available and no longer meets the definition of secret.

As part of the joint status update, Ramacciotti asked the court to hold a status hearing this month, during which Apple would be required to say what additional information it still needs from him. He also wants Apple to have 30 days at that point to either drop its claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial.

Apple, meanwhile, wants to continue with document discovery, including a second deposition of Ramacciotti and efforts to compel the documents Prosser has yet to produce. Prosser argues he has met his agreed-upon document production obligations and is resisting Apple's ongoing requests for more material.

If Judge Donato doesn't grant Ramacciotti's request for a status hearing, the parties suggested another joint status report be submitted on December 2.
